speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: CHANGES IN DEPARTMENTAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
In the forthcoming year a number of changes will be made in programs of the Department of Agriculture so that the maximum assistance can be given to producers with the money which has been allocated to the department under the government's policy of budgetary restraint. These will include program adjustments, curtailment of travel, construction and acquisition of equipment, controlled expenditure on some cost-sharing programs, and increased fees for certain services performed by the department. Changes are aimed at increasing efficiency of operation and at terminating or reducing longstanding programs which have tended to reach their objectives or the applicability of which has become less appropriate in the context of current departmental and governmental objectives.
Adjustments in programs will, of course, cause adjustments in staff, particularly since there will be staff expansion for programs providing essential services to the public and, as indicated above, for those of high priority. Thus, while staff reductions in most cases will be met through normal staff turnover and staff transfer within the department or government service, there will be some lay-offs of staff employed on lower priority programs.
A start on farm adjustment programs is planned as well as the rapid expansion of CANFARM, the national farm management program.
In order to implement and expand these programs, adjustments will be made in the support provided to dairy and sheep producers. For 1970-71, $115 million is being budgeted for dairy support. These changes in price support will provide between $10 and $11 million.
I should note that the wool support level will be continued during the current year at 60 cents per pound.
In the research program there will be a continuing policy of work realignment. The following specific actions will be taken: experimental farms at Mile 1019, Alaska Highway, Yukon Territory; Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories, and Caplan, Quebec, will cease to function as research farms of the department.
In the production program there will be the elimination of grants to a few organizations and less funds available for the loaning of beef sires. The specific associations will be advised where grants are being eliminated. Another step will be taken in the new year toward the previously announced phasing-out of hog premiums. The premium of $3 will continue to be available but only on higher index hogs effective January 5, 1970.
Two open-end, cost-sharing programs are under review and for the new year a ceiling will be placed on these expenditures. These are the assistance programs to fairs and exhibitions and the federal-provincial 4-H programs. Discussions are being, or will be, held with the appropriate representatives so that the action to be taken can be as satisfactory as possible to all concerned.
Fees will be increased for certain services to bring them more in line with the benefits that accrue to the individual obtaining these services. The ones to be adjusted in the new year are: record of performance (dairy cattle), seed potato inspection, ship inspection, field inspection of certain crops, shipping-point inspection of fruits and vegetables, the registration of certain products and facilities, and the inspection and quarantine of animals.
The nature of the actual change in the programs for those items where I have indicated only a reduction in expenditures will be announced at an appropriate time as well as the details concerning the changes in the costs of services, etc. In the meantime consultations will be undertaken with applicable groups in order that their views may be obtained as to the most appropriate use, in keeping with the objectives of the program, which can be made of the funds that are to be provided in the forthcoming year.
November 18, 1969

Agriculture Program Changes
In conclusion, may I say this is the first time the department has announced well in advance-several months in advance-the changes which it is intended to make in these programs. We hope this early notice will be useful not only to members of the House but to the public who are affected, enabling them to make their views known to us before the date on which the changes are actually made.

Mr. Speaker, this announcement by the minister amounts to nothing more than a statement couched in flowery departmental language saying, in effect, that for the sake of political expediency the department is sharply curtailing its expenditures during the coming year. It means that at a time when agriculture is facing its worst problems of development, the government is withdrawing from research, withdrawing services to the farming communities, and withdrawing from subsidization programs indiscriminately. We find it is even shutting down some experimental farms.
The government has indicated that there is going to be some shifting of staffs and perhaps some lay-offs. Experience has taught us that this will disrupt the entire department. It is unfortunate indeed that at a time when agriculture most needs help the government is withdrawing from its responsibilities and obligations. May I also point out that this announcement today is in direct violation of all the advice sought by the government at the congress that they said was so successful last spring.

subsubtopic: CHANGES IN DEPARTMENTAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we had more days for opposition motions perhaps we might receive more statements of policy. This statement is notable in that it provides no hope for positive action for an industry that is in trouble. The adjustments proposed are negative. It is not a forward-looking statement. It will not give the farmers confidence that the government has a grasp of the problems facing agriculture and is determined to do something about them.
The statement indicates that a start is to be made on adjustment programs, but we will have to wait to see just what these adjustments are since the statement itself does not give any details. Adjustments are going to be made in the support for dairy and sheep producers, but all we know is that cuts are going to be made somewhere.
The whole tenor of the statement is that cutbacks are going to be made in the depart-

ment and in the services to people who depend on the department. In other words, the document simply is an innocuous one which gives no hope to agriculture and farmers for the immediate future.

subsubtopic: CHANGES IN DEPARTMENTAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I cannot congratulate the minister on the statement he has just made.
Right now, in eastern, central or western Canada agriculture is in trouble. The minister's long statement will bring us another deception since it tends to provide maximum assistance to producers with the credits allocated to the department under the government policy of restraint. In fact, the minister seems to say that we will grant more subsidies with less money.
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad that in 1969, a Minister of Agriculture as competent as the present one could not turn aside from the beaten path and suggest a financial policy in accordance with the overabundance of products our farmers are able to offer the population.
In the field of dairy products, for instance, we are not facing a production surplus, as indicated in the statistical data of the federal government, but rather a problem of under consumption.
The minister has also announced a curtailment of travel expenses. We could understand that but, on the other hand, he said that subsidies of $115 million will be granted to the dairy industry to support the price of milk, which will result in savings of $10 or $11 million for 1970. This means that in April 1970 our deception will be more bitter on account of the quotas on manufacturing milk.
I regret that in 1969-70 we have no better announcement to make to farmers than this unfortunate statement which bears no relation to the progress and problems of agriculture in 1969.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) has done me the honour of seconding my motion.
If there had been any doubt whatever in my mind about the wisdom of making such a motion it was completely dispelled by the statement the minister made this afternoon on behalf of this so-called government, a statement which amounted to nothing less than a declaration that the government has closed the doors on attempts to solve the major problems facing agriculture today and is resorting to an undignified retreat from its responsibilities and obligations. It is my considered opinion, an opinion shared by all my hon. friends on this side of the House, that these decisions were taken solely for reasons of political expediency in a desperate attempt to balance the federal budget without giving consideration to the implications as they affect the agricultural industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
During the past six years we on this side of the House have tried desperately to bring what is happening in agriculture to the attention of the government. We have pointed out that the industry is in a flux of evolution. We have pointed out that measures which might have met some of the problems to a certain extent prior to 1963 are no longer sufficient to meet the demands of 1969
DEBATES	937
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies and 1970. We have tried to make it clear to members of the government that the problems which bear on agriculture today affect every field of Canadian life-that the consumers are directly affected by price changes and food costs, that health and welfare measures are directly concerned when farmers are forced to leave the so-called poorer farms of this country and migrate to the urban centres to become, for the most part, welfare cases; that the Department of Labour is concerned when it is called upon to find employment for these people or retrain them because they can no longer make their own living on the farms.
Especially during the past months we have sought to bring home to the government the fact that agriculture as a whole is in dire financial straits, and whenever we have done so government spokesmen have attempted to prove that the gross income of the farming community was much greater than ever before and that the net income is growing every year. I contend this is just a method of book-keeping which is used by government supporters to conceal from the Canadian public as a whole exactly what is happening in the agriculture industry. It makes not one bit of difference if a farmer receives 5 per cent more gross income during a year if his expenditures rise by 10 per cent and if his interest charges have increased from 6 per cent to 11 per cent in a single year; his "take-home" pay is far less than it was a year earlier. It is hard to convince such a man that he has never had it so good.
Isn't it strange that when we point to one of the greatest industries in Canada, the industry which exports more goods than any other, the industry which employs more people than any other, we should find that the increase in the inventory value of the holdings in that industry has, over the last ten years, been almost identical with the increase in borrowings by the industry from government sources? Speaking from memory, I think the figure is around $1,800 million.
Through the years the government has indicated to leaders in agriculture that it is aware of the problems and is attempting to do something about them. The fact is that today leaders of farm commodity groups and farm marketing organizations are no longer coming to Ottawa to present the facts, make their requests and offer advice and suggestions to the government. They have found from bitter experience that all they get is a pleasant hearing and absolutely nothing else.
Most of us concerned with agriculture were invited to attend the agricultural congress,
November 18, 1969
938	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies and for this we thank the minister for his courtesy. In his opening address, which was excellent indeed, the minister stated that the three main objectives of the congress were, first of all, to deal with matters realistically; second, to approach the problems in a practical manner, and third, to look at agricultural needs not in the short term but in the long term. This is very commendable.
The minister also indicated to the assembly that he was not interested in political expediency but in the long term approach to agriculture that he, as minister, wished to adopt. In other words, he left the impression-and I admire him for this-that he was not interested in extending his own political career or the political life of his party; he was acting solely for the good of agriculture.
Within three weeks, contrary to every indication in the congress report, the minister took it upon himself, without consultation with the industry, to reduce the subsidy on the hog program, one which he had said 90 days previously had been formulated after consultation with the industry. The minister reduced this subsidy unilaterally, without consultation even with the members of the agricultural committee in whom he said he had greatest confidence. The minister took it upon himself to reduce this subsidy in order to cut expenditure in the Department of Agriculture.
This is the man who said we must speak with realism, in a practical manner, and deal with the long time good of agriculture. If this sort of action is repeated, there will be no farmers and no need for a long term policy. The Canadian agricultural industry as such will be finished.
There is no doubt that this congress, to which all leaders of agriculture and allied industries were invited, reflected the desire of the government progressively to withdraw from the financial support of agricultural institutions and to drop, as I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) put it, the paternalistic approach to the industry. Otherwise, how could the government, which has been supporting the agricultural industry in Canada for 100 years, now tell that industry it is no longer interested and is going to withdraw its support? I say the government cannot withdraw and will not withdraw.
An indication of the government's intentions was given the other day when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) stated in this House that preferential tariffs were going to be applied by Canada and


developing nations to the mutual benefit of both. Those who have engaged in agriculture or any of the allied industries know that the prime exports of developing countries in the world are agricultural products. It talks about those small farm operators making $2,500 a year, as though they have no right to be on the farm any more. We are facing a new age. There are going to be far more farmers living on farms making under $2,500 a year than there were in the past. This is the type of farmer who will accept full or part time employment in an adjacent city. He will, because of the high cost of living and inflation, be forced to do both jobs. This type of existence is not the exception, it is rapidly becoming a way of life.
In the interests of farmers as a whole, the government must reach the decision that we camiot have any over-all legislation for farmers. It must recognize that there are three distinct types of farmers in this nation for whom something must be done. First, there is the large commercial entity composed of a number of groups of farmers banding together for the purpose of operating a common feed plant, a food processing plant or a cattle feeding operation. That is one type.
We then have the family type farms. My definition of a family farm perhaps differs from that of other hon. members in the House. Under today's circumstances, a family farm is a farm that utilizes to the "nth" degree every possible mechanical and technical advantage but where the labour input exceeds that of purchased labour.

Finally, we have the small farmer who lives on the fringe of suburbia or an urban centre in which there are commercial and industrial enterprises. He augments his income by working in the factories or in industry. He might even drive a school bus in order to provide, in his own fashion, for his family.
The government cannot adopt one policy in respect of these three types of farmers. These people have various problems, both agricultural and social. This government must make a decision. Perhaps during its term of office it can make one decision. It must decide to put farmers in training programs and provide adequate employment so they can furnish their families with the necessities to which they are entitled. The government must evaluate the cost of such a program and decide whether it would be cheaper for the taxpayer and better for the welfare of small communities to introduce programs which would keep the small farmer and his family on the farm. It is very easy to say we are going to retrain this group of farmers in order to move them into the cities where unemployment is increasing even for those who are specialists, and where we have not got adequate housing. Under this program we would put farmers out of their homes, which would fall into disrepair very quickly, and put them into other areas which also have problems. The result will be to increase the problems of the small municipalites which will lose their tax base and thus be unable to support community life.
We have a Liberal government today which, after nearly seven years in office is still trying to ascertain the problems. This is the same Liberal party that assured the people in 1963 it knew all the answers. Seven years later we are staggering blindly along unable to reach concrete decisions, even after months and months of deliberation. The policy the government has evolved amounts to a withdrawal of financial support from the agricultural industry, and a withdrawal of its responsibilities and obligations. It proceeds with blind faith that perhaps tomorrow will be a better day.
I have no confidence in this government. I have no confidence in the plans it has put forward for the future of agriculture. When I note that the very knowledgeable leaders of this agricultural industry in Canada refuse to come to Ottawa because they feel that would be of little value, I am sure that standing in my place here I speak for the Canadian farmer.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion and in due course will move an amendment. I am amazed that within the year, or better than a year now, that this government has been in office it has not brought before this House a clear enunciation of a policy to meet agricultural problems as members of the government see them. A year ago members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture looked at the agricultural scene in Canada. During that study members of the Standing Committee, not only of the opposition but also of the government, agreed there was a necessity to take a look at what was happening to the farming industry in Canada. So, we travelled to western Canada and to eastern Canada. Some areas still remain to be visited. The committee has not even yet made its final report. Members were ready to comment on some of the things they saw. I am sure there were some things upon which members of the committee, in their extended tour, could have agreed to make recommendations to the government of the day. As a result of their tour, the members of the committee did recommend some things to the government, very few of which have been implemented.
When we met here on September 23, I thought one of the top priorities for the government would have been to have this committee meet, bring in a final report on eastern Canada and cover some of the very important issues on which the committee has not yet reported. One of these issues, notably the feed grain situation, was left until the committee made its final report. The government, however, apparently feels there is no urgency for action in this particular field, otherwise it would have acted. Yet, I do not suppose there is any facet of agriculture in which there is a greater disarray or a worse situation than that which exists in respect of feed grains in western Canada today. One hears of farmers selling feed grain, wheat, oats and barley, at prices that are simply give-away prices, such as 50 cents and 60 cents a bushel for wheat. One wonders how those who buy this feed grain have the gall to go into the yard, load it up and haul it away. But I guess there is no limit.
One hears complaints, some of which were also heard by members of the standing committee. It was obvious from our discussions with the officials of the Board of Grain Commissioners that feed grain was bypassing the regular trade channels and

November 18, 1969

appearing in eastern Canada where it offered competition to those manufacturers who made their purchases through the Wheat Board. In view of this situation one would have thought the government would have considered it urgent to ask the members of the committee for advice on how to deal effectively with the problem. But no, that was not done. If the government did not want the advice of the members of the committee, then one would be led to believe the government itself would make a proposal for dealing with the situation. But, no. So, like Mohammed's coffin, the problem hangs half way between heaven and hell, waiting for someone to bring it down to earth.
As members of the committee travelled about the country there were other things they saw which required attention. One of these was the abattoir in Nova Scotia which is seeking to deal with the problem of marketing livestock in Nova Scotia and perhaps part of New Brunswick. This abattoir is in need of some aid for its effort to serve that area. But I suppose this problem also has been lost in limbo. One could go on and mention other things we saw on that tour, such as the change that is taking place in agriculture. After looking at the big processing plant in New Brunswick, we could see the close tie-in there is now between marketing and production. Policies are needed to deal with this situation. Only this morning representatives of the National Farmers Union appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to ask for consideration of the high interest rates which now prevail and with which farmers are trying to deal and live. Some farmers will not be able to cope. I do not know the number of farmers who will be in extreme difficulty because of the interest rates which now prevail in Canada.
Some sectors of Canadian business and Canadian industry probably will be able to live with this type of interest rate structure without too much difficulty. I would not venture to pass an opinion on that, but I will venture to pass the opinion that agriculture will not survive and be healthy with the interest rate structure which it now faces. That same interest rate structure will prove to be one of the factors that will prevent the adjustment to other forms of production which some farmers are having to make in Canada today, and more particularly in western Canada. A farmer is a pretty flexible individual. He can adjust to a great many
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies different conditions. He is pretty resourceful, but the one thing he cannot adjust to is a zero income. That is what many farmers in Canada are trying to do today; they are trying to adjust to a zero income. This is impossible.
I could provide figures, but why bother. They have all been quoted in this House before, and, indeed, many times during the last year. Is it necessary to put more on the record? I doubt it. Perhaps a brief example might be sufficient. Last spring the price of beef was $35 per hundredweight. When it reached that point the head of one of the great chain stores in Canada advised that there should be a boycott. One minister said he thought this would be a good idea. Well, it was effective within six weeks. The price went down to the neighbourhood of $29 and now is down to $28. Some farmers who put cattle in their feed lots last spring will be lucky when they bring them out this fall if they are able to repay their loan. These are the men who are attempting to adjust to a new set of circumstances.

Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies
I proceed to read from an editorial which
says:
The thing that bothers us is this: the present farm income situation is such that government failure to introduce sound and effective policies immediately will be disastrous. We may assume that Mr. Trudeau's farm policy statement was in line with his concept of a "just society". Farmers in this case can scarcely be blamed for being totally disillusioned.
That is the feeling out in western Canada. This government could not elect a member on the prairies today if there were an election, and in that I include the Minister of Agriculture who crept in by 400 votes the last time. They know that and still they will not act.
Here is what the Winnipeg Free Press says:
The problems of the Canadian farmer today are usually associated with a slumping market for wheat. Certainly this is the number one problem, but it is by no means the only one. The whole agricultural economy is in bad shape and it has not been improved by the policies of government or the advice of the experts.
There has been no guidance to the farmer, and may I read the exact words? ". . .he received no guidance on these matters." The reference is to the question of what he should or should not produce or what alterations he should make.
He continued to produce high quality wheat and, as recently as two years ago, was advised to increase his production.
And so it goes, down the line. Western Canada's dairy market has been destroyed by this government and by the tinkering of the Minister of Agriculture. Here is what the article says about that:
Even dairy production has its problems. When Canada had a huge butter surplus, farmers were urged to reduce their production of milk for manufacturing purposes. Western farmers did this; those in the east did not. Now with fixed quotas the order of the day, all the large quotas are in eastern Canada; the prairies caught in a strait-jacket, are no longer allowed to produce enough butter for prairie needs.
No longer allowed to produce sufficient butter! That newspaper, the Winnipeg Free Press, can never have ascribed to it the heresy of Conservatism.
Every year Manitoba is forced to import millions of pounds of butter from Quebec-butter on which the western consumer has to help pay the subsidy as well as the freight. In the meantime, unable to get quotas, thousands of milk and cream producers in the prairies are being forced out of business every year.
That is true. What is the government doing about it? In effect, the minister says, "That is the rule and we cannot change it." But they can change it, so why don't they?
November 18, 1969

Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: You describe it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Does the minister not receive hundreds and hundreds of letters from dairy farmers in western Canada protesting this injustice to them?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: And from eastern Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: I know, and from eastern Canada too. That proves exactly the point made by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth). Things are bad in eastern Canada, too. I thank the minister for that interpolation. Out of the mouth of babes comes wisdom. The minister has again proved that aphorism.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Don't exaggerate the situation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
What about the wheat situation? The hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt is apparently satisfied, but I intend to refer to the position in which we now find ourselves. Canada, in the last year and a half, has lost its reasonable and fair share of the world wheat market. It has fallen by approximately 9 per cent or 10 per cent. At the same time the United States is increasing its share.
I have before me an extract from the Southwestern Miller of Kansas City dated September 23, 1969 which reads:
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Bookings of flour and wheat for export last week were largest in some time, and additional sizeable volume is pending. Major business in flour was purchase by A.S.C.F. of 1,318,000 cwts of bread and all-purpose flour for October export relief. Bookings by Brazil and Japanese Food Agency comprised major portion of export wheat business.
The article goes on to tell of the increases. The United States sold to Saudi Arabia, Bahrein, Congo, Dominica, by barter as a matter of fact, to Colombo, the Netherlands, Surinam, Honduras and a tremendous amount to Brazil. While all this was happening the government of Canada stood back and did not give to the Wheat Board the support that it should in order to assure that Canada got its fair and proper share.
There are those who criticize the Wheat Board. I am not one of those because if it had not been for the Conservative party, there would not be a Wheat Board. The Board was established by the Bennett government in July of 1935. The Liberal party did everything they could to throw monkey wrenches in the way to prevent the implementation of that act. Then, for a period of years-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Which one was that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Agriculture was not a member of the Liberal party at that time. I recall he was one of the directors along the line and I am now referring to when he sat in a more accustomed place.
There have been nine months of waiting with regard to Communist China. I am not going to discuss the cowering attitude of the government of Canada as it goes before Mao and asks for the right to recognize the government of Communist China. I ask, what are they going to get? What is a quid pro quo? Are they going to sell extra amounts of wheat to Communist China? Do they know? We were able to bring about sales as a result of extending credit at a time when recognition was not even regarded as being within the realm of possibility.
The same is true of Australia. Australia is getting the orders, but they wait. I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) if during these deliberations in Stockholm, either on the street or in some building in Stockholm, he were discussing the possibility of Communist China buying wheat. Do we get any trade out of it? Not a bit! Those countries that have recognized Communist China have not increased their trade. What was the reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs at a time when we have over a billion bushels of wheat piled up? He said, we have not talked about wheat. I suggest these two ministers should get together with the Secretary of State for External Affairs and point out to him that there is a market that might be secured.

speechtext:
I always appreciate acts like that, but they always have the result of making it impossible from then on to be in any way seriously critical.
I feel that something has happened in connection with the Wheat Board. I think the ministers of this government sit in the shadows and are not giving support to the Wheat Board. They are playing around and giving lip service. The whole problem of wheat marketing must be reviewed. There can be no delay.
November 18, 1969

The other day I asked the hon. Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt whether consideration was being given to setting up a royal commission. He swept that aside by saying, no, we do not go in for that. Well, there were more royal commissions under the Pearson government and since the present government came into office than in any similar period of time. The minister said that today we have task forces. What is needed today is a royal commission to investigate the whole marketing problem and to place the responsibility for the loss of Canadian markets abroad where it deserves to be.
One of the reasons the government is opposed to setting up a royal commission, a commission which should be able to report within a period of three months, is the fact that they realize such an action would be a condemnation of this government. The statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) "If you expect me to sell wheat..." was an obvious and clear indication of the attitude of this government.
I mentioned something about the problem of sales. Imagine the advertising Canada received through an article which appeared in the Wall Street Journal headed "Bartering with grain helps Saskatchewan weather wheat glut". The article states the only way prairie merchants can keep alive today is by bartering wheat. It mentions one merchant in the city of Regina, a furniture dealer who, because of the serious shortage of cash was unable to sell his merchandise. Having learned either to swim or drown, he now barters furniture for wheat. This is happening all over the province. While this happens government members simply smile and smirk.
Why doesn't the government do something? Members of the government have been out west. They have left with the farmers the hope that something is going to be done. When the Prime Minister returned to Ottawa his words became clear and definite, "Do you expect me to sell wheat?" The situation on the Prairies is critical beyond words. There has been nothing to equal the fear and frustration that exists with these people today. When they look to tomorrow, they wonder what is next. They have a right to expect action.
Now then, what is the reason for this situation? Is it the Wheat Board? The Agricultural Economic Research Council of Canada brought the Canadian Wheat Board under fire for alleged timidity in the struggle for world grain markets. It emphasized the serious
DEBATES	947
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies situation that is resulting through the failure of the Wheat Board, as I understand it, to get out of the tentacles that have held it back in the last two or three years and to start to sell wheat.
What about the possibility of persons or organizations outside of Canada selling our wheat? Why should there be organizations from every country but Canada endeavouring to get orders for wheat? There is a list of five or six of these international traders. Let us give private industry the opportunity to go and look for markets. Other nations have these corporations in various other countries. It is time we in Canada did something similar.
I will conclude by simply summarizing what I have endeavoured to suggest to the House should be done. First, we should have aggressive policies for sale and not just the evasive answers we receive in this House for failure to act. Second, there should be an acreage payment of $2 an acre-something the wheat farmer has a right to expect under present conditions, third, the implementation of a system of farm storage involving accelerated depreciation of multiple-use farm buildings in addition to that already in existence. Next, we should give to the farmer market outlines and guidelines in co-operation with the provinces which would enable him to know the direction in which the industry is moving and to make the most effective use of his land, farm resources and labour. Fifth, the government should improve road and port facilities-and use Fort Churchill, extending the period during which Fort Churchill can be used. By putting modern technology into effect, the port could be open for at least six or eight weeks longer during each season. Let the government do this. It would mean a saving to the western farmer. It would also mean the use of the installations we have there, facilities which are virtually not being used at present. Twenty million bushels or so a year does not begin to cover the situation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I think the time has come when sales of all wheat for domestic human consumption by the Wheat Board should be fixed at a price of $2.95J per bushel. I remember that when the hon. member for Medicine Hat was sitting in the Social Credit party this was something he advocated. He wanted a two-price system and he advocated a responsible price for the wheat which was used in Canada.
November 18, 1969

Finally, there should be on the part of this government a four year commitment of more than $100 million to be used for assistance, development and adjustment of the prairie farm economy. Some have asked for more. I believe this amount, if used properly and appropriately would bring about a rejuvenation of agriculture in western Canada. I say to this government: if you do not act you will encounter a revulsion of feeling in western Canada on the part of responsible people, people who follow the law, such as I fear to mention; you will add to the fires of that group which today throughout western Canada is preaching secession. It is becoming a subject of discussion. It must be met. It would be met if this government would take off the shackles which have prevented some of its members, however estimable they might be, and however desirous of action, from doing that which in their own hearts they realize should be done.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of my contribution to this debate I want to say something by way of rebuttal, if that is the right word, of the charges which have been made by those who have taken part in the debate so far. What is more, I have been invited by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) and by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) to make some comparisons as between the five years immediately past and the five years preceding them. Each of those hon. gentlemen repeatedly referred to the fact that this government had been in office for five years. Then they went on, I suppose, to deprecate the record during those five years. Perhaps it would be as well if I were to make some of the comparisons they suggested, focusing them on the particular periods to which hon. members opposite referred.
Before doing so I think I ought to say a word or two about the statement I made on motions earlier today because, as usual, it has been interpreted in a completely contradictory manner by hon. members opposite. Just for the record, and, perhaps, for their information, I should like to ask them to read


some of the observations I made a little more carefully. Obviously, they have not done so. If he would look at the statement I made

opportunity to make representations and express their views as to the best way of making the adjustments. Now, I should like to turn to some of the matters which were discussed by hon. members opposi e. Since hon. gentlemen opposite have this uppermost in their minds, I will have to spend some time on it.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Dan-forth) repeatedly suggested that since the government took office in 1963 allegedly terrible things had been taking place. In response to that statement made by the mover of the mo'ion I think the appropriate thing to do is to make some comparisons on either side of the year 1963, say five years before and five years after.
The average cash income from sales of wheat in the years 1958-62 amounted to $464,378,000. The average between the years 196468 was $715,255,000, an increase of 54 per cent. The average cash income from the sale of oats in the period 1958-62 was $26,334,000. Between the years 1964-68 this cash income rose to $30,226,000, an increase of 14.8 per cent. Cash income from barley during the first period was $70,595,000, and this rose during the second period to $84,570,000, an average increase of 19.8 per cent.

Hon. members opposite also mentioned rapeseed, and I should like to put on the record the average cash income from rape-seed sales during these periods.

Hon. members opposite also complained about rapeseed sales, but I would ask them to look at the facts. The average cash income from sales of rapeseed during the years 195862 amounted to $11,180,000. The average for the period 1964-68 was $35,632,000 an increase of 218.7 per cent.
I do not have time to put all the figures on the record, although I should do so. I will have to content myself by making a quick reference to the relative increases.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a note dealing with that and I will come to it. The hon. member will have an opportunity later in the debate to deal with this, that is, if he has done his homework. I hope that somebody on this side will be able to follow him and straighten out some of his twisted statistics.
With regard to soybeans, the average cash value showed an increase between the two groups of years I referred to of 54.7 per cent. The increase in the cash value of corn between the two periods was 139.2 per cent, and for potatoes, 38.8 per cent. Fruits showed an increase of 48.8 per cent. These figures do not represent tonnage but cash value to farmers from the sale of these products.
Let me put on the record some other statistics in which hon. members might be interested. The increase in the cash value received by farmers from the sale of cattle and calves between the two periods I have referred to has been 46.2 per cent. Income received from hogs has increased by 24.9 per cent, dairy products by 20.1 per cent and poultry by 46.3 per cent.
I now come to another matter with regard to which hon. members have not done their homework, the federal government deficiency payments. The average annual deficiency payment made by the government during the period 1958-62 was $2,692,000, compared with $6,421,000 for the period 1964-68, an increase of 138.5 per cent. In addition, of course, there was the dairy program, a program that was non-existent when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office. I am sure that any reasonable person, looking at the facts, would agree it is obvious that the comparisons between the years either side of the year 1963 invalidate the arguments that have been raised. I am not saying that things are going well in all sectors of agriculture.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: You said that the farmers had never had it so good.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: No, I did not say that at all. I have heard the hon. gentleman attempt once in a while to put those words into my mouth, but without success.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: That is what you are saying right now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
I am not. What I am saying is that there has been an increase in the cash

flow received by farmers from the sale of their products, and the hon. gentleman knows that is a fact.
Let me just restate the motion that has been moved:
That, in the opinion of this House the government has failed in its duty to the Canadian farmer by its neglect to initiate and promote adequate marketing and distribution of food and agricultural products and the adoption of effective international policies with respect to agricultural commodity arrangements.
Total Canadian exports and exports of agricultural products to all countries, by major groupings, are as follows. Again I am using the year 1963 as the pivot. Between 1958 and 1962 average exports of all commodities amounted to $5.4 billion. The average between 1964-68 went up to $10.2 billion, representing an increase of 89 per cent in Canada's exports of all commodities. With regard to agricultural products, average exports between the year 1958-62 amounted to $1,052 billion; the average between 1964-68 increased to $1,607 billion, or by 52.7 per cent. The argument is not valid that there has not been a very significant increase in the export value of Canadian agricultural products.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
After putting those facts on the record, I want to comment on some of the other matters we are also dealing with, and which urgently need some intensive attention because they relate to these problems. There is orderly marketing, for example of farm products. There have been many serious attempts, I suggest, in the past by both individuals getting together and through their groups-co-ops, or whatever they call them- as well as by governments both provincial and federal to introduce more orderly marketing of farm products in this country as well as exports. There has been an attempt to rationalize production with consumption.
I can understand a lot of the difficulties that people have been confronted with in the past in trying to resolve these problems. The division of powers under the constitution is one of them. I do not believe that we in agriculture should wait, however long it may be-a matter of a few months or a few years -in order to obtain complete agreement among the 11 governments on the constitutional changes necessary to accomplish a new division of powers which would enable us to overcome these problems. We can continue the negotiations which we have been carrying on in a more active way, I am told, in the
November 18, 1969	COMMONS
last year and a half than has ever been the case before. Indeed, I have had five meetings with all the Ministers of Agriculture across Canada or their representatives in order to work out the problems we will have to meet in respect of these constitutional difficulties.
I say that because it will not be good enough to attempt to pass legislation, regulations or an administrative authority based on the present division of powers if someone can successfully take us to the courts and have such legislation ruled ultra vires of the federal jurisdiction. Such action has been tried in the past. We want to do this in co-operation with the provinces. As I have said many times, we think the best course to follow is to ask this house for enabling legislation under which we can set up a marketing council and, subsequently, particular marketing groups, agencies commissions or boards, whatever they may be called. We can then set them up under that legislation in such a way that these specific commodity groups can receive delegation of power from both levels of government. We could then get around the Constitutional problems and attempt to bring in legislation that exceeds the authority in this area.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: That is an amazingly new idea.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
It is not all that new, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has indicated. Let me say to him that I think this time it is going to work, maybe because cooperative federalism is now at its best. Mr. Speaker, I should like to open my remarks on the no-confidence motion made by the Progressive Conservative party not only by
DEBATES	953
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies blaming the government for not having taken the necessary action to assure the farmers of a fair share of the national income, but also by making suggestions for the building of a truly just society for every social class and for every category of workers, including farmers.
It is disappointing to realize that from year to year the farmer's share keeps on decreasing.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has quoted meaningful figures and I think he has proved his honesty by refuting the charge that the government did not take the required steps to solve that problem.
Undeniably, attempts have been made, but without succeeding in making the farmer derive more profit from his work, from his efforts to participate in the national activity, producing the foodstuffs required by the population.
I would like to give an example of concern to both housewives and meat producers. The steadiness of retail prices of beef over the past three months reminds us of the gradual rise in the marketing costs of foodstuffs. Among these costs, a difference must be made between the price to the consumer and the price paid to the farmer.
It is common knowledge that a 1000-lb. steer on the hoof cannot supply 1000 pounds of prime steak. The ratio is in the vicinity of 125 pounds, or 10 per cent of the total weight of the animal. But nobody understands that the retail price of a very good roast is kept at the supermarket at the level of June last, namely $1.59 per pound, while from mid-June to the beginning of October, the price of steer on the hoof decreased by some $10 per 100 pounds.
The middlemen, and in particular retailers, submit that none of their customers has to buy beef at $1.59 per pound; there is a wide variety of cuts, less expensive from which they can choose. To that one could retort that no customer has to believe either that a grocery store is right to keep the price of its beef at the same level while the price of a steer decreases by $10, at least on the hoof.
Yet, all those people in the trade: commission salesman, slaughter house operator, wholesaler, retailer, in short all of them dismiss that responsibility.
The fact is evident: grocery stores quickly and often boost prices whenever farm prices go up ever so slightly. Conversely, retailers
954	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies seldom pass reductions on to customers when farm prices go down. This trend does not apply to beef only; it goes for all foodstuffs and is more prevalent as years go by.
It is logical and normal for processors and bank agents-the intermediaries, in other words-to receive more today than yesterday because they have more expenses, wages are higher, packaging has improved, processing is more elaborate, the food is pre-cooked, etc. However they have taken the necessary steps to increase their profits by raising their prices to consumers.
In fact, all increases in retail prices are absorbed by the intermediaries. None of them reach the farmer. Yet, God knows how much production costs have climbed. Interest rates are also higher. You will recall that during the last session bills were introduced in the House for the purpose of modifying interest rates on farm loans. Ceilings were lifted in order to allow financial institutions to get better returns on their money.
But these higher interest rates are a contributing factor in the increased production costs of farmers, and as the latter are unable to recuperate these higher production costs when they market their commodities, they inevitably suffer a reduction in their income. This is what we are now complaining about and it is the reason why we would like to see, besides current measures, additional steps taken to guarantee to the farmer the possibility not merely of keeping body and soul together for a while, but also of enjoying a decent standard of living.
When asked why the interest rates were raised, the minister answered that the financial institutions no longer agreed to make loans at rates of 5 or 6 per cent as they brought them no profits. I remember telling the Minister of Agriculture that the government was much more anxious to please high financial circles asking for higher interest rates because of allegedly insufficient profits, than to satisfy the farm people who, for the same reasons, asked that prices be raised to provide them with a better income.
As far as we, the farmers, are concerned, we stand in a somewhat unique position. We cannot indefinitely store farm products. Indeed, we have to market them, whether the sales are profitable or not, and to suffer the losses as they come.
Farm machinery costs more also. So does mill-feed this year, especially since the subsidy for the transportation of feed grain from
[Mr. Lambert (Bellechasse) .1

west to east has been reduced to $1 a ton. The minister did not mention it a few minutes ago, he did not have the time. In any event, this is one of the factors that contribute to the increase in production costs. I am asking the Minister of Agriculture if it is all possible for him to come back on his decision, in order to facilitate the transportation of feed grain that the western farmers would be quite happy to sell to the eastern farmers, but at prices that will enable the latter to produce meat, eggs, etc., at reasonable prices while still making a profit. This reduction will necessarily have disastrous effects on the Canadian economy.
From 1949 to 1967-I know it is always boring to hear statistics, but it is thanks to them that one can make fair comparisons- the volume of marketed food increased by 74 per cent but, quantity for quantity, marketing costs increased by 137 per cent according to a federal government document. In 1949, Canadian consumers bought food for a total of $2,064 million. On that amount, $1,243 million were returned to farmers. The middleman's part amounted to $821 million, that is 40 per cent. Now, in 1967, the retail value of food sold in Canada exceeded $5.9 billion on which $2.5 billion, that is approximately 43 per cent, were returned to farmers and nearly $3.4 billion, that is 57 per cent, to middlemen.
This is one of the causes that could explain why the condition of the farm workers deteriorates every year, as is clearly shown indeed by the continuing decrease in the return share that ought necessarily to go to farmers or producers.
Finally, I blame the government for doing nothing to improve the lot of farm producers, in order that they may get a fair reward. I do not say that the government does absolutely nothing, for this would not be true, but I do say that they must be guaranteed a fair reward for their work, so as to be assured of an income at least equal to that of their fellow-citizens who work in other sectors of the economy.
In the dairy industry, the curtailment of subsidies and the increase in the export premium on the 1968 equivalent production constitute by themselves a cause for the deterioration of the economic situation. The influx of ersatz products that threatens both the consumers' health and the farmers' future-

We therefore require the public, the consumer to co-operate, in order that he may be well aware of what he is buying and able to compare it with Canadian manufactured dairy products.
Several agencies, agricultural and otherwise, have put forward very valid suggestions to help the government in solving problems.
Once more, I would like to urge the Minister of Agriculture to see that the Standing Committee examines as promptly as possible all briefs submitted in order to evaluate the suggestions put forward, particularly by the C.F.U., the Quebec Federated Cooperative, whose thoughtful and well prepared briefs offer a solution for the problem of milk surpluses. In fact, those agencies ask for a distribution in the schools. This suggestion could be examined. I think it is a sensible suggestion. In the United States they do that and, as far as we know, there is no waste. What are the terms? I do not know. But, at any rate, I should like to invite the Minister of Agriculture and the officials of his department to examine that policy in order to determine whether it could not be applied in Canada. Would it not be possible to distribute these food products in homes and charitable institutions whose resources are not sufficient? Moreover many families have an insufficient income. One should not imagine that I am referring to the governor of the Bank of Canada who already gets a sufficient salary and is not compelled to deny himself, because he has a purchasing power which enables him to meet his needs. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened this afternoon, as have other hon. members, to a variety of speeches on the motion and the amendment before the House. I was glad to hear at last the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who asked that we face reality and examine the problems affecting agriculture.
I must say he did not sound like members of his own party earlier today; this was not the tone used in the past by far too many politicians in his own party and others. In recent times, far too many people were interested in speaking about the agricultural situation in tones of complete optimism or in terms of unmitigated, unavoidable disaster. It was as bad and as wrong to talk about the situation in language of unrealistic optimism, to overlook information, already available, about the changing situation, persuading farmers to ill-advised courses of conduct with regard to their equipment, land assembly, and so on, as it is today to speak as though the situation has no possible solution and disaster is inevitable.
The truth lies between these extremes. The situation is indeed serious; in the eyes of some of the farmers facing it, it is overwhelming. It is important for the government and for all associated with the agricultural industry to look at the situation realistically and to give both leadership and hope to the farmers who face these difficulties most directly.
The gloom expressed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is not helpful. Nor would it be helpful to
960	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies pretend that there was no information available to counter some of the optimistic statements which were made in the past. I would refer hon. members to the outlook papers of 1967 and 1968; in each case the experts indicated that the production of grain would probably continue to outstrip sales and that increases in stocks would take place accordingly. There were some who were interested in taking an optimistic view and whose urg-ings of different courses overshadowed these forecasts. This in itself contributed to the surplus, the presence of which is so direct and so overwhelming to the farmer who faces it.
We in this government are firmly confident that there is a significant and happy place for the farmer and his farm in our society. We are satisfied that the problems which confront him can be attacked and dealt with when they are examined realistically. I should also like to say that this government stands four square behind the Canadian Wheat Board. We do not hesitate to say this flatly. We shall not use the weasel words of some hon. gentlemen opposite who say they support the Wheat Board and then point the finger of dark suspicion at something which seems, they infer, to be influencing it. Those may be proper tones for people who intend to destroy the Wheat Board, but not for those who are determined to support it.
There is no doubt about the seriousness of the situation facing the farmer. This has been recognized by the government. The government has been on record on this issue for many months past; we are on record as recognizing the problem created by the surplus, by low prices and by high costs as these seriously affect the industry in the area of grain production and, more particularly, of wheat.
I would refer hon. members to the statement made in August by my colleagues the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) which referred to the cash position of western farmers, indicating at the same time that the government would hold the price of wheat on the domestic market to that fixed under the International Grains Arrangement. This is the one price which we can, in fact, control. This statement also recognized that the government must keep a constant watch on the cash position of farmers. We were aware that though the cash advance program would provide immediate

DEBATES	November 18, 1969
cash assistance, it would not solve the cash shortage over the period of a whole year. I refer hon. gentlemen to the portion of the statement in which this is recognized.
I should like you to know, Mr. Speaker, the way in which the flow of cash advances is moving. According to the latest report I have, on November 14 the figure stood at $227 million, or slightly more, an increase of some $2.5 million over the previous week which itself represented a rise of some $5 million over the preceding week, and that was a rise of $8 million compared with the week before that. This indicates the nature of the cash flow under the cash advance arrangement.
It is important to remember that in these circumstances the farmer is facing difficulties arising from many factors around the world including the total world production situation. We should bear in mind that in the past four years world production exceeded ten billion bushels each year: It had not done so before and, indeed, it increased to that figure from an average of 8.6 billion bushels in the previous four years, a production which itself represented a new plateau.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It is important to remember that world trading in wheat decreased last year compared with the previous year as a result of the increase in production of wheat by exporting countries, but more particularly by countries that might normally have purchased wheat from the wheat exporters. Canada's share of the world wheat market held up amazingly well under these strains. It is true that our total sales of wheat, for instance, dropped from 335 million to 305 million bushels. At the same time, total United States exports were dropping from 760 million to 543 million bushels, and Australia's exports dropped from 256 million to 195 million bushels. I do not suggest that these figures solve the farmers' problems, but they do recognize the magnitude of the task of accurately calculating sales prospects, dependent as they are on conditions all over the world.
May I repeat what the Minister of Agriculture said and which the Leader of the Opposition treated so lightly. We must do the best possible job of ascertaining market prospects and keeping the farmers informed. We must look realistically at the very fundamental question of how large a grain inventory we should carry in this country. We should also look at the results of our examination rather
November 18, 1969
than, as has happened far too often in the past, simply ignoring them.
Both the government and the Wheat Board have been working very hard to expand our sales internationally and to bolster prices. I should like to remind hon. members again that we have had a trying time in regard to world wheat prices. But this country has faith in international grain agreements. We believe they make economic sense, and that we exercised very significant restraint in the face of breaches of the agreement by some of our competitors. Eventually, when we could not persuade them to return to the minimums, on March 14 we indicated with reluctance that we had to meet their prices even though this meant going below the IGA minimums.
The result has been that the exporters of the world have seemed to learn the lesson that no one gains from that particular game. I am happy to be able to report that as a result of very hard work, and following a period when we might have been quite pessimistic, progress is now being made toward the stabilization of world wheat prices. I am confident that any future movements in price will more likely be in an upward direction.
I would also mention a few other things that have been done in the cause of improving both wheat sales and the lot of the grain producer. For example, there is now a regular form of credit such as that used in sales to Poland and China, and under which government liability now stands at $200 million. An additional credit facility has been made available for sales by the Canadian Wheat Board. The sum of $6 million is included in the estimates of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to enable lower interest rates to be used in areas where commercial sales cannot be made at regular rates. By using this facility recently a sale of 5.5 million bushels was made to the Philippines, which was a re-entry by Canada into an important market. Even more recently there was a sale of 7.5 million bushels to Peru.

It is important that the farmers understand and appreciate this fact, and that they have the appropriate amount of hope.

I could refer to the transportation system which has taken up so much of our time in the past year or so, and the development of the block system-that imaginative forward step in the movement of grain from the local elevator to the terminal. Where the block system has been put into effect, it has worked extremely well and gives every indication of living up to its promise in allowing the expedition of the movement of much more grain than was possible under the previous helter-skelter system. The block system is now in effect in over half the prairie region and will be in full effect before the opening of the navigation season.

It is in that context that we will have to look at the question of oats and barley and the extent to which they should be fully on quota and fully controlled as Wheat Board grains. I would remind hon. members that when they refer to distress selling of these grains under the Wheat Board, it is by and large, a transfer of benefit from one type of agricultural producer to another and is itself reflected in certain distortions in the cattle industry. For instance, the price of feeder cattle, which is high compared with the price of finished animals, is perhaps a distortion; but it indicates that the producer of meat does indeed benefit from these distressed prices. No one says the prices are tolerable at their low level; they are in themselves a sign of the serious situation which faces the farmer.


It is important for us to create conditions which will not lead the grains producer to dispose of his inventory of feed grains at prices at which he could not possibly replace that inventory. It is in this context of quotas and these fundamental questions that we will have to look at the question of how best to handle rapeseed, flax, and so on. We will also have to look at these questions from the point of view of enforcement problems in regard to quotas. We all know that the quota system has been badly breached in the prairie region in terms of producers complying with it. It seems to me that in the immediate future we must encourage farmers to follow the rules such as they are, even while they are being re-examined. A breach of the rules leads without doubt to unfair distortions in favour of those who break them, and at the expense of those who do not. It is, therefore, a very important matter economically to many farmers.
In conclusion I should like to say just a few words about prospects. We will hear more about this matter before the month is out. Present indications are that this year's sales of grains will meet or exceed last year's totals. Barley sales abroad will surely go above last year's total, and wheat sales could and should, indeed, be somewhat higher depending on certain specific developments. But this-I wish to emphasize this point- does not mean that the problem of the surplus is a quickly vanishing one, because we are all aware of and must remember the size of the surplus on the farms and in the elevator system.

Ever since I have been here, whenever we have had a debate on agriculture it has been a patchwork one. I suggest that even the Minister without Portfolio, who at least tried to come to grips with a few basic issues, gave us facts and statistics of what the government has tried to do on an ad hoc basis, putting its thumb in the dyke like the little Dutch boy. The government is trying to cure this problem by giving a little advance here and helping out the farmer there. But these are only reaction policies, reflex actions. There has not been any positive policy to begin with; that is where the real problem lies. The government has not stopped to ask itself some basic questions and to set out some basic objectives of an agricultural policy for this country.
The government has not even posed the question: What is the place of the family farm in this country? It has not asked itself what should be done with the surplus wheat and the blossoming and expanding production of soft cereals in markets where former importers are now exporters of grain. Is there going to be freedom for the farms, or shall we let the government control and dictate policies? What are the trends of farm production for the future? What do we do with export excess? What international policies do we have, if any? Can we produce without subsidies? This is a very urgent problem in the east.
Do we have production in some areas that is to the detriment of other areas? Do we produce for and distribute to the developing nations sometimes to the detriment of their own production? These are some of the questions that should be asked by the government, which should develop policies in answer to them. But no, those questions have not even been put.
We all agree that the country is changing, indeed the world is changing. Hopefully, men will land on the moon at one o'clock this morning, and yet we are still talking about the policies and fighting the election battles of 1962, 1963, and 1965. We are not talking about future policies with a view to helping us elevate our sights-not as high as the moon: we do not want to get to the moon; the cow
November 18, 1969
jumped over the moon years ago and people may have gone over the moon in expectation of what this government would produce after June, 1968. As the leader of our party said today, all we want is the Minister of Agriculture to at least come to the House and be candid with us and with all Canadians from coast to coast, as was the Minister without Portfolio who started to tell us about the problems and the difficulties of agriculture.
Men on this side of the House know as well as the minister does and as their geographical mates do, even though they may be political enemies, that there are problems in agriculture which may not be insurmountable but which are difficult to solve at this time of change and transition. There is a movement from the farms to the urban areas; there is consolidation of little units into big units; there is an advancing technology which has developed production beyond our dreams of 20 years ago. But even allowing for this transition and change, agricultural policies cannot be turned on and off, as was said in the pathetic statement made by the minister today with regard to further changes.
I could make a whole speech about the minister's sentence in which he said there will be cut-backs in agriculture because of the present policy of austerity. I suggest that it is penny wise and pound foolish to strike at such a basic industry as agriculture and make cut-backs in this area when it takes many years to develop a milk herd, production facilities for grain, drying facilities or any other element of agriculture. One does not start a program one year because there is a surplus or a deficit in the national budget and then change the whole program next year because, owing to the munificence of the Minister of Finance there is a little extra money available with which to help the farmers.
The two announcements made recently have caused confusion and concern in the agricultural community. I refer to the turning on and turning off of policies and to the two most recent statements on agriculture made by this government. One statement was with regard to the dairy policy which was to become effective on April 1, 1969, and the second was with regard to the hog premium policy which was to become effective on March 31, 1969. In the case of the dairy policy, farmers across this country were given one day in which to readjust to the new policy. So far as the hog premium policy was concerned, they were given the grand total of six days before the policy became effective.
965
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies
I am not arguing the right or wrong of either of these policy changes. What I am saying is that even if you are a Member of Parliament trying to organize your mixed-up life between the House of Commons and your constituency, between being here, in your constituency, in your office and attending committee meetings, you have to plan a little. If you are a business man, you also have to plan, so why expect something else from the farmer? He has to plan also. He has to plan a longer time ahead than just season to season. But in two basic elements of agriculture, the dairy industry and the hog industry, the farmer was given one day to adjust to the new policy with regard to the former and six days to adjust to the latter. I suggest that this does not show the concern that we have heard professed by members opposite, and we cannot believe them when they say they have a sense of reality about the agricultural situation in Canada.
In the few minutes I have remaining to me I should like to direct my remarks, not to the over-all situation in the west because there will be others more familiar with the intimate details concerning the west, but to the problems confronting farmers in the east, be it Ontario, Quebec or the four Atlantic provinces. There are in these areas farmers who are going through the same transitional period and the same changes. The figures here and there may differ greatly; they may involve a few acres to a few hundred acres as compared with a few hundred acres to a few thousand acres in the west, but the relative problem remains the same. It is the same for the man who is trying to work the land. These men are not afraid of the challenge of change. They are prepared to meet it. But they do not want that challenge of change compounded by confusion within the Department of Agriculture, by constant reviews by either the task force on agriculture, committees or all the other study groups, let alone by the retreats in policy which we heard announced today or the two changes in policy to which I referred a moment ago.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
But because of these elements there is very deep concern in the east, and in the far east, with respect to three particular matters. One of these is the feed grains policy about which the minister made an announcement a few weeks ago. The second is the question of export markets, which is one of the basic areas to which the motion is directed, and the third is the question of imports into Canada

S66	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies which affects farmers in the east, in the central parts of Canada and elsewhere. We would like to know just what the future will be for the farmer on P.E.I. growing potatoes, for the farmer in the Saint John valley, and the farmer in the Annapolis valley, which I have the honour to represent. Where do we go with respect to poultry, eggs, and potatoes, not to mention apples?
Dealing first with feed grains, I do not suppose there is any other policy in agriculture that involves as many political cross-currents as the feed freight assistance act whereby the eastern producer gets feed grain from the west so that he can develop an industry in the east. In the 28 years since that policy was developed in 1941, a viable livestock industry with all the products inherent therein has been developed in the east, and so much so in the province of Nova Scotia that livestock and products, including poultry, make up 80 per cent of the total farm income and form the basis for any further expansion.
There are conflicting problems involved. You have the western producer to consider, the Ontario corn producer and the eastern farmer who must have transportation help known as feed freight assistance. A viable policy has been developed, and even though it has involved political cross-currents it is fundamental to the east. If we are to have any meaning behind the purpose of regional development-which is one of the two things a certain gentleman parroted around the country in June, 1968-we must realize we have to walk carefully before change is made in any fundamental policy such as that respecting eastern feed grains. Unfortunately, confusion has developed in the Department of Agriculture, and among certain farmers, between the question of feed freight assistance and a viable land use development policy.
The result is that some people in Ottawa think that since eastern farmers are arguing about a land use development policy, designed to utilize the land in more progressive ways, they may discontinue or discard the eastern feed grains policy. If that ever happens, and if some of the inklings recently dropped by the minister bear fruit, there would be a backward, negative reaction in tbe eastern farming community, so great that a whole new department of regional economic expansion would be required to take care of that problem alone.
However, it appears that we will not have any viable land use development policy for some time, because everything is being cut

DEBATES	November 18, 1969
back by the government. But let us not confuse that issue-particularly when we consider that we have so much land use in the west that the result is that grain is piled up sky-high-with feed freight assistance for viable industries that are producing such a large amount of farm income in the east, particularly in Nova Scotia.
There is another area I know something about, Mr. Speaker. It concerns export markets, and here I have particular reference to the apple industry in the east. It covers other commodities but I am more acquainted with the apple situation. Here I refer to national marketing policies. Again the minister has dropped a few tidbits to the effect that some time some statements may be made on national marketing policies.
We need some direction, not only on national marketing policies within the country designed to control cut-throat competition between one part of the country and another but also on external marketing wherein this country must face the subsidized products of other nations. Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian producer is meeting subsidized products from France, Germany, Italy-you name the country and it has its subsidized products. I want to know what policies the government has to encourage and develop export assistance for our producers in meeting competition in outside markets. Another element which causes concern in the east is the importation of concentrates, either in the form of apple-paste or tomato-paste-
