This House awaits with interest the definir tion of new policies. If the Minister ;lqf Agriculture will stop playing musical chair? with old figures and past battles, and instead develop new policies to meet some of the
November 18, 1969	COMMONS
problems that have been increasing in perplexity over the years, he may be pleasantly surprised at the reaction from this side of the House. There is not a member on this side, or in fact in any part of the House, who does not appreciate that we are talking about a basic industry, agriculture, and that it is no good seeking short-term partisan political gain when talking about something so fundamental to our country. All Canadians, whether they live in the cities or on the farms, have a vital interest in the agricultural policies that the government should be announcing and which we are awaiting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to discuss agricultural problems and policy, as I have done at every opportunity since I became a Member of Parliament in June, 1968. I can agree with many things that have been said by the mover of the motion, the mover of the amendment, and by some other opposition speakers. But I must take strenuous exception to a statement made by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) who early in his remarks said he was moving his motion "on behalf of the farmers of Canada." What an unmitigated presumption! He cannot produce any mandate from the farmers of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
He certainly is not speaking for me, and I am one of the farmers of Canada; and he is not speaking for a great many other farmers whom I know. I was also surprised to hear the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) speak so disparagingly of myself, a backbencher on the government side. At other times, when it suits him, he poses as the protector and champion of the backbencher. He sought to give the impression that I never got on my feet in this House. As some hon. members know, I have spoken out in this chamber on numerous occasions on behalf of my fellow farmers. However, I am not surprised that he is not aware of this, because I do not recall his presence in the House at any time when I was speaking. In fact he is not here tonight, and about the only time he is present nowadays is when he has something to say himself.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert wept crocodile tears because some farmers were selling their wheat at reduced prices.
I believe he used the figure of 50 cents per bushel. Mr. Speaker, I was farming in the early thirties when the Conservatives were in 21362-62J
DEBATES	967
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies power both in Ottawa and Regina. Nobody came to my yard to pick up my wheat at 50 cents per bushel I hauled many loads of wheat, with horses, five miles to the elevator and received less than 30 cents per bushel.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: You are pretty old.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
I am. It is true that the Bennett government established the Wheat Board on its deathbed in 1935. But it was set up on an ineffectual, voluntary basis, on a renewable five-year term. It remained for succeeding Liberal governments to make the Wheat Board effective by requiring all wheat to be marketed through it, and later giving it responsibility for barley and oats. In recent years, too, a Liberal government put the Wheat Board on a permanent basis. Mr. Speaker, the farmers of western Canada recognize that these are the actions of a government and a party that is fully committed to the Wheat Board system of orderly marketing. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) this afternoon reaffirm that stand.
The opposition further damages its credibility as a possible alternative government by condemning this Government in such sweeping generalities in the motion we are discussing today. The mover of the motion had no alternatives to present. It is the easiest thing in the world to court popularity with those people who are in difficulty, by loudly criticizing the government. This is one of the favourite indoor sports of many people. It is quite another thing to propose workable and practical solutions. These were notably absent so far today from opposition speakers.
My remaining remarks will be directed to the grain producing sector of the agricultural economy. It is the area of agriculture that has the greatest problems. The situation is not good, but to say that it is worse than ever before, or worse than it was in the thirties, is completely absurd. In 1967-68 we exported 336 million bushels of wheat. In the 13-year period, 1950-51 to 1962-63, this total was exceeded in only four of those years, 1951, 1952, 1960 and 1961, two years under a Liberal government and two years under a Conservative government. In 1968-69 our exports dropped to an estimated 306 million bushels, which is about 26 or 27 per cent of the total exported by the four main world wheat exporters that year. That is about the same percentage of the world wheat trade which we experienced from 1959 to 1963.
968	COMMONS
Alleged. Lack of Agricultural Policies
Most farmers are encouraged because of the appointment of the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) as minister with exclusive responsibility for the Wheat Board-the first time a minister has been given exclusive responsibility for the Wheat Board. This was the immediate action of the government in response to the statement made in the Speech from the Throne that steps would be taken to maximize sales of grain. The Wheat Board says it is doing everything possible to sell grain, and I know the new minister will give it his undivided assistance and encouragement.
The government has taken the advice of farmers and farm organizations and appointed a farmer, Mr. Charles Gibbings, to the Wheat Board as of last July 1. If there was any need to have a farmer's viewpoint heard within the councils of the Wheat Board, we certainly have it now. This was an extremely commendable appointment and it demonstrates the government's concern about the needs and wishes of farmers.
As on previous occasions, I am going to take this opportunity not only to praise the government for some of the many positive things it has done, and is doing, such as doubling cash advances, making them available on unharvested grain, making interim payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, crop insurance programs and stimulating credit sales of grain, but also to offer what I believe to be constructive criticism of various policies.
I should like to refer to the deferred delivery plan, under which farmers who were prevented from delivering the promised five-bushel quota last year were to be given permits to deliver the balance during this crop year. When the plan was first announced it provided that no farmer could deliver more than one bushel per specified acre, no matter how far short of the five-bushels he might have been. That unjustifiable and unfair restriction was removed and I learned just this morning that the limit has been set at two bushels. Let this be the opening shot in my campaign to have this arbitrary restriction removed.
In many remote areas on out-of-the-way branch lines, the elevators were almost constantly plugged throughout the year. Farmers who were at some distance from their elevator, who had no phone or who happened to be ill on the wrong day, had great difficulty getting their grain in. Remember that at many of those points the quotas were still at one,

DEBATES	November 18, 1969
two and three bushels in June and even into July. I find it completely understandable and believable that many farmers had grain on hand but were unable to deliver even three bushels per acre. Now these same farmers are being arbitrarily cut off at a maximum of two bushels.
They had already been three-time losers, in comparison with the majority of farmers who were able to sell the five-bushel quota before the end of July because (1) they lost the use of the money they should have received for several months; (2) they now take over 20 cents a bushel less on their initial payment, and (3) they had a much larger storage problem than their more fortunate neighbours. I think that the last that should be done is to allow them to deliver the full amount they were short of five bushels on July 31, and to assure them that they will ultimately get at least as good a price for wheat delivered in 1969-70 as they would have had they been able to deliver it in 1968-69.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: What does the minister say to that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
Another point I wish to mention has to do with the current supplementary quotas on durum and barley, and any new supplementary quotas which may be announced. Last year such quotas were unceremoniously cut off at a predetermined date, even though many farmers did not have an opportunity to deliver their grain because of the lack of space at their delivery point. They were understandably incensed at losing this eagerly anticipated income opportunity because of the vagaries of boxcar distribution.
I protested this insensitive attitude most vigorously last year, and I was afraid there might be a repetition this year. However, I am pleased to note that the Wheat Board has now agreed to extend the durum quota to the end of July and has decided to suspend, perhaps temporarily, the special quota on feed barley, which may be reinstated later this year when barley stocks become depleted. I like to think that my representations in this matter have had some effect, possibly through thie new minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
I would like to revert to the deferred delivery plan for a moment and register my objection to deductions from the cheques for these deferred deliveries, to be applied on cash advances, when there was no liability existing on account of cash advances as of July 31,
November 18, 1969	COMMONS
1969. These deductions are a further discrimination against those who were prevented from delivering their five-bushel quota last July. It might take a slight amendment to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, but I understand it is to be opened up very shortly anyway for amendments having to do with advances on unharvested grain; therefore, this small amendment should cause little difficulty.
I should now like to make a few remarks about box car allocation. I think the authorities responsible, mainly the railways, did a terribly poor job in this regard last year. There was the excuse last year that the tough and damp grain upset their procedures, but so far this year there is no such excuse. When I am critical of the railways in this regard I am not alone. When the agricultural committee interviewed the Canadian Wheat Board in Winnipeg on April 18, 1968, 1 asked the chief commissioner if he thought the railways should take some blame for the poor distribution of box cars last year. He said, and I quote from page 1257 of Report No. 32 of the Proceedings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
I certainly do. We cannot direct the railways on where to put their cars. We have no power. We can direct the distribution of the cars between the elevator companies and the stations and I certainly want to go on record that I am not congratulating the railways on their distribution of cars between stations but, in the over-all, we cannot direct them on this.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
In my opinion, confusion and discrimination still exist in the distribution of box cars. As some hon. members know, I asked for and received a meeting with top railroad officials. This was discussed last evening during the adjournment debate on a question raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Sko-berg). I attempted, unsuccessfully, to correct the quotation the hon. member used. The quotation listed some of the people who were present at that meeting. It mentioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister without Portfolio in charge of the Wheat Board. It mentioned members of parliament from the prairies, including myself, and some prairie Senators. The omission 1 wished to correct was the fact that one Member of Parliament, the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) was also at the meeting. The railways were represented by four of then-top executives, including Mr. McMillan, president of Canadian National Railways and Mr. DEBATES	S69
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies Gossage, vice-president of Canadian Pacific Railway, in charge of rail operations.
It is true that no opposition members were there. I believe we had a very frank and beneficial exchange of opinions and ideas, probably much more so than would have been the case if opposition members had been present. I think there have been indications in the past two weeks that some improvements are now in prospect, and indeed may already be evident in some areas.
The block system which will soon cover the prairies may be an improvement, but I think we farmers should not be under any delusion that the block system is designed to allocate box cars more fairly between points and between farmers. It may do what it is meant to do, namely, make better use of our rail system and our country and terminal elevator systems. I hope it does, because this will benefit farmers generally. However, farmers are individuals and require, deserve and expect fair treatment. I intend to do my best to see they receive that kind of treatment. If discrimination and hardship continue to be visited upon individual farmers and individual communities, even under the block system, I will renew my request for a transport controller.
We need a national policy for Canadian agriculture. It is long overdue. The report of the task force on agriculture is due within a few weeks. The government would be subject to justifiable criticism if it proclaimed a comprehensive farm policy before this task force makes its report and before the new Canada Grains Council has a chance to make any recommendations. I am sure the opposition would be foremost in such criticism. I look forward to some significant policy announcements by the government in the next few months.
Also needed are more reliable forecasts of production goals and some realistic programs to assist farmers to diversify in order to meet these goals. I was pleased to hear today from the ministers that steps are being taken to provide this guidance and assistance. I renew my plea to the government to support the price of wheat at $1.95J for export as well as domestic consumption. Agriculture is in great difficulty, mostly because of world conditions, but I do not think it is quite as bad as this exaggerated motion tries to indicate. I will not support the motion, Mr. Speaker, or the amendment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have heard the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) on a number of occasions state what in my opinion is probably a fairly good assessment of the problems of agriculture. I have never seen the particular hon. member put his vote where his mouth is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
If the hon. member knows these things are wrong, obviously he should not stand as he has tonight and whitewash the department. I have no objection to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) doing that, Mr. Speaker. I remember when he was a colleague of mine. We were both opposition members and both spokesmen for agriculture. I always listened carefully to the Minister of Agriculture as he understood many of the problems of agriculture in Canada. His difficulty now is that he is taking instructions from a department. He is not really facing the problems of agriculture in Canada today; he is selling policies that have been developed in the department for which he is responsible.
The Minister of Agriculture could do a great service to this country if he made a break with tradition and decided to raise in this House a number of problems which he knows exist. If he honestly listened to the arguments surrounding the problems he raised, he could formulate a new program. The last speaker stated there is a problem in the world today, especially in western

Canada, of having more produce than we can sell.
It has often been suggested that the problem in Canada is not producing wheat, but selling it. This has been a fact since the 1920s. I am sure the minister and the hon. member for Assiniboia know this. What is being done about it? I have listened to these problems being discussed for 10 or 11 years. I have often heard the silly remark used by the previous speaker, that if we cannot solve the problem any other way, we will appoint a transport controller. Why have we not appointed one? Every time we had a problem with boxcars in the past we appointed a transport controller, and when the problem was solved he was dismissed. If this has always solved the problem, why the hell do we not have a permanent one?
This is a small problem, but I am sure the Minister of Agriculture and the former member for Assiniboia talked a great deal about box cars. I am sure there have been more discussion in this House on the subject of box cars and the inequality to western farmers caused by the inability of the railroads to have the box cars at the right place at the right time than there has been on any other subject. The hon. member represents a riding in western Canada. He says that if the problem cannot be solved in any other way, he will agree to the appointment of a transport controller. What kind of representation is that for western Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext: Just a big bubble.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-LACK OF EFFECTIVE AGRICULTURAL POLICIES
speechtext:
It is obvious the hon. member will vote with the government. Why? I am not sure why. I really would like to know why. There are many problems in agriculture, Mr. Speaker. The problem we are faced with today is that we have a surplus. We have often had a surplus. I was surprised to learn that Ireland has a surplus of agricultural commodities. I understand they are selling butter to Chile at 11.8 cents a pound. The problems of agriculture are not the same as those in industry and other fields. The problems in agriculture are over-production and inability to sell.
The Minister of Agriculture has known about these problems for a long time. I am sure the minister responsible for the Wheat Board also knows of them. If he does not know of them, he need only turn to his desk-mate who for years has been connected with the selling of grain. These are the people who make their total fortunes from selling grain.
November 18, 1969	COMMONS
It is a complicated problem. Obviously there will be trouble attempting to sell grain at a given price in a glutted market. However, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the new department, whatever it is called, have been coasting in this respect.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I think everyone would agree that we should put some money into our efforts to sell agricultural commodities. We should be honest about what we do with wheat. The Wheat Board does not sell wheat; James Richardson & Sons sells wheat. The brokers sell it, but the Wheat Board does not sell it. In my opinion, McNamara never sold a bushel of wheat in his life, though he has sold other things. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is a good salesman. It seems to me he might well do as other ministers have done, including a former minister of trade and commerce now sitting to my right, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), and call together the people responsible across the world for the operation of our trade. When it was last decided to put on such a campaign, sales were made. It is true there was a lot of mumbo-jumbo about who actually made the sales, but we did embark upon a policy of salesmanship and it was successful.
We shall always have bumper crops periodically in Canada, and the more plentiful harvests will probably fail to coincide with years in which the largest sales are made. We must therefore find some way of equalizing the returns.

speechtext:
They can go out and have a conference. Their way of solving this problem was to pay the farmer a cash advance. The hon. member for Assiniboia said he would recommend that they go back to last year's quotas, and that he would press for this. He is not being honest. He has already done so, and the Wheat Board has told him to go to hell. I got this information from his own paper, the Assiniboia Times. We are now dealing with dilemmas which face all governments, not only the government in office. I suggest the minister would do well to turn his attention to solving some of the long-term difficulties. His department will give him all kinds of reasons why nothing can be changed, but I put it to him that he should examine some completely new propositions.
DEBATES	971
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies
One of these would involve the provincial governments. If hon. members believe that agriculture is in trouble only in western Canada, they are wrong. The same difficulties arise from coast to coast, stemming from our ability to over-produce and our failure to sell. The agriculture committee travelled from one part of Canada to another, and during these journeys, I, as a member, learned of the great change which has taken place in eastern agriculture from the individual farm unit to the agro-industrial complex.
The family farm was in trouble because the farmer could not get enough for his produce to pay the cost of producing it. When the cream cheque is not providing enough to pay for the farm, or when the cheque for fluid milk is not large enough to enable a farmer to keep going, the whole industry is in desperate straits. There are, I suppose, some farmers who can carry a certain proportion of the burden of a low income by cutting their standard of living still further, but the big businesses are geared to producing at a high level of efficiency for markets which offer them a certain price-and if this price changes, the industry is in an extremely difficult situation.
Take the broiler industry and consider its relationship to egg production. Quebec controls the production of broilers and Ontario controls the production of eggs. The interests of egg producers in one province can be played against those of the broiler producers in the other, to the point at which the agencies which have been set up can no longer make a reasonable profit. I was surprised to learn that in Quebec they are not interested in establishing marketing boards for the various commodity groups. The provincial minister of agriculture said he was not interested in establishing a marketing board but that he would support any proposition which the federal government might have to put forward in this field.
Surely, the minister has heard similar stories from the conferences which have been held. Surely he is aware that this bugaboo about the constitution is not the barrier it used to be. We have learned that this is the case, and we shall tell him so if he allows the committee to make a report. If he is willing to bring in marketing legislation on a national scale, the provinces will accept it. This is the only way in which we shall be able to operate effectively.
We, the people of Canada, should be responsible for the orderly marketing of our

972	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies agricultural produce. Today, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) indicated we should cut back production if a market did not appear to exist. But how in hell do we cut back? Suppose a wheat farmer has a thousand acres lying idle: the minister says he should plant only 100 acres because a good market does not appear to be likely. So far no provision has been made for a guaranteed annual wage, and unless he puts in a crop, this farmer will be on welfare.
Already the Wheat Board is selling wheat at prices which will not pay for the gasoline and the costs of putting the crop in and taking it off. Meanwhile, much of the grain remains on the farms. It may be cash in the bank, but the farmer would like to spend some of it; he is not getting enough cash to carry on. The minister is advising him to take land out of production. But is he telling us, at the same time, that he intends to announce a greenbank program? Almost every country in circumstances similar to ours has decided to embark on programs designed to take certain agricultural land out of production with provision for its use later if that should be in the national interest.
No such program has been announced here. In the meantime, who will keep our farmers if they do not plant grain? Who will pay back the cash advances we made available this year on top of the cash advances which were extended last year, advances which in many cases have yet to be repaid? The government would have us believe that these cash advances are a wonderful thing. I suppose it is a wonderful thing I should be able to go to Household Finance and borrow money, but I would do that only if it were really necessary. In the long run there is nothing particularly beneficial about getting cash advances if one has no way of paying back the money.
The only reason farmers get these cash advances is that they would be unable to keep going at all without them. The minister knows these things. I listened to him talk about them for years when he was on this side of the House. Now, apparently, he finds it easier to have the deputy minister and the departmental officials give him advice as to how he should run his department than for him to determine what is really in the interest of Canadian agriculture and make policies accordingly.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) decided there should be an austerity program and that some programs should be cut. One of the first things to suffer will be the agricultural


fairs throughout the rural communities, which are the show places of agriculture. The minister is also going to suspend grants to the 4-H clubs, which are junior farmers' clubs. These clubs teach our farmers of tomorrow the skills and crafts to enable them to operate farms. If the minister beheads all the farmers, he will certainly solve their problems for them, though the nation would hardly be a contented one. However, every few years the public have an opportunity to make then-decision. Revolutionary ideas of this nature would produce counter-revolutionary ideas, and the result would not be as anticipated.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Let us not talk about what this person did or that person did, about the lean years and the fat years. As far as farmers are concerned, every year is a lean year. I have not heard one farmer admit that times were good. Even if times were good, the farmers would not admit it because they know that the next year will not be good. Looking back over the past 50 years our farmers have not been wrong yet.
I suggest to the minister that long-range programs are required. The minister's policy in regard to the cream producers and farm separated milk has resulted in half of the small farms in Canada going out of operation. In my own area even a farmer on an unproductive piece of land cannot be driven off his farm. You cannot help him, neither can you hurt him very much. You just cannot get rid of him.
Almost $2 billion has been lent to the farmers for the purpose of developing economic farm units. I suggest we have an obligation to ensure that the products the farmers produce are sold at a reasonable profit, and that farmers are able to operate viable units. Let us talk not about yesterday but about tomorrow. One of the worth-while things that the minister did was to organize the agricultural congress. At this congress the minister heard about the problems of the farmers and how they could be solved. In spite of this, not one solution has been presented to the members of the House for their support. I suggest this is what the minister should be doing in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, now that we are debating agriculture I observe it is opposition day again. I have been engaged in agriculture all my life, and having listened to this debate it seems to me that the abilities of an organized group of
November 18, 1969
individuals who through the years have been the backbone of Canada are being downgraded. Hon. members suggest that since the farmers do not know what to do, we should tell them. They suggest that the farmers overproduce because we tell them to; that they are unable to appraise a given situation and have to come to us for guidance.
What the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has been trying to do for a year or so now is to give the farmers an opportunity to express their problems. He invited them to the agricultural congress. He has visited agricultural communities. The agricultural committee has traipsed around Saskatchewan walking in the fields and talking to farmers. We have seen financial statements of farmers and we are aware of their problems. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has visited the west, where he was pelted with wheat and shown obscene signs. I was talking to a young man from Saskatchewan the other day who told me that those involved are still apologizing to Canada for some of the actions that took place during the Prime Minister's visit. These people were not necessarily farmers. In fact, I would be prepared to say that they were not farmers but agitators who claimed they supported the farmers.
Agriculture today is experiencing a revolution; indeed, it has been for the last five or six years. The farmers have realized that technological advances have made over-production possible. They also realize external aid has meant that the underdeveloped, needy countries have been enabled to produce the agricultural products they need. The farmers know there is a world wheat problem and that something must be done about it.
Certain sectors of the agricultural industry have done something about this problem. I should like to inform the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) that the broiler industry in Quebec is not controlled as it is in Ontario. Every province but Quebec has a marketing system for broilers. The price of these broilers is higher in the rest of Canada than in Quebec simply because there is no Quebec marketing board and broilers are being over-produced. Broiler growers in the rest of Canada are operating viable farm units. This means that banks are prepared to lend them money. No longer are they so dependent on farm improvement loans or the Farm Credit Corporation. In consultation with government officials they have evolved a broiler industry that pays. The same can be said of the egg producers. A few years ago
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies there was over-production and the price was low. Today eggs fetch a good price, and this is because the egg producers got together and solved their particular problems.
I recognize that hon. members of the opposition are sincere and dedicated to the agricultural industry of Canada. I refer particularly to the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth). I say this, not because he is bigger than I but because I meet him in the agricultural committee and I went to Saskatchewan with him, along with the hon. member for Timiskaming.
The Minister of Agriculture cannot be expected to shoulder all of the problems of the agricultural industry. But he does want to talk over his policies with the farmers to see whether they are appropriate. As hon. members know, the government is proposing to introduce some national marketing legislation, and it has been criticized for not bringing it in sooner. I wonder whether hon. members realize why this legislation has not yet been presented to the House. The reason is that the plan is still being discussed throughout the length and breadth of the land among the farmers themselves. How many members of the opposition can show me a copy of the draft of the national chicken marketing commission act which has been presented to Department of Agriculture officials for their consideration?

How many hon. members have investigated that aspect? This matter will be considered by the government in a very short time. How many hon. members have visited these people?
Let us consider the situation facing the hog industry. I have heard talk about cutting off hog subsidies. This was never considered a hog subsidy. Very good breeders in my riding have told me they never considered it to be a subsidy; it was an incentive or bonus to breeders who improved the quality of their hogs. That is all it was. If you produce a better hog, you get more money. The idea of subsidizing a hog grower for producing a poor product is simply outdated. You do not subsidize a chicken grower who produces eggs at a loss but makes a profit because the government picks up the tab. That idea has gone by the board. The same argument applies to the turkey industry.
Let us now consider the problem facing the grain industry. I realize it is a tough one. I

It was stated earlier that we lacked the ability to sell our product, that we overproduce and undersell. That is the phrase used by the hon. friends. There is another phrase we can use: we over-produce and under-consume. There is just no way you can shove food down the throats of people. We keep referring to the fact that a great percentage of the population of the world is starving and hungry. We realize this. Members on this side of the House are just as responsible for this situation as anyone else. You are members of a political party, Members of Parliament, and when and if you come up with a really bright idea and turn on a 500-watt light which lights the way to a proper distribution of world food, without wrecking the economy of underdeveloped and other countries, you will be surprised at the reception you will get.

I received a letter just the other day from an old colleague of mine who is in the chicken business in Spain. One of the first things he said was: Jerry, I am in Spain and we have a problem here regarding the over-production of broilers and eggs. Would you get a hold of some of your marketing board acts and the natural produce marketing acts and send them to me so that we can find out if we can do something about this?
Only a couple of weeks ago I received a reply to my letter, saying that in Spain they had invoked a marketing act and a marketing board in order to handle this surplus. I was told today that there was a surplus, believe it or not, of chickens in India. Of course, these chickens are perhaps not too good by our standards. I am not sure they are particularly edible, but there is a surplus. There are surpluses everywhere because we over-produce and under-consume. The main problem is created by an under-consumption of the products we produce. We should produce to a market.
We have a peculiar situation in the House of Commons today. I do not intend to take up much more time because I know there are others who want to speak, but let me liken this situation to what takes place on a football field. On an opposition day hon. members on this side seem to pick on agriculture, and there is no greater political football than the situation in which our agricultural industry 

finds itself. This bothers me because I am a great friend of many of those who do a great job to produce food for people here. Unfortunately, you sit here and tell them they are doing everything wrong. There are problems, but as long as you insist on telling them they do everything wrong the problems will continue.
It is surprising that a number of members in the opposition who represent grain farmers keep telling them they do not know what they are doing. They insist that the government should be telling these people what they must do in order to operate their businesses successfully. This whole business reminds me of a Grey Cup game; we have interceptions, we have piling-on and we have interference. The only thing we do not have is a scoreboard, and we will probably get that before the evening is over.
Let me refer to an article published in the Western Producer. It states in part, under the heading "Favourable report for UFA despite farm income problem", that their financial position was reported by the United Farmers board of directors at the opening session as having been assisted by sales of $24 million, which is $2,635,000 more than the year before. Let me refer to another article which appeared in the Western Producer which refers to what Mr. Turner, president of the Wheat Pool, had to say, as follows:
To those who say the board should have sold more last year he pointed to the high world production and lower world trade in wheat and said that in the face of these adverse conditions Canada's exports actually represented an increased percentage of the total in 1968-69 over the year before.
Again I should like to commend the hon. member for Kent-Essex for bringing this subject to the attention of the House. I could not possibly agree with the wording of his motion. I would not except him to commend the government; although I am new here, I do not think that is done by anyone in the opposition. As a member of the agriculture committee I know we have a big job ahead of us this year. We must do what we can. When we are planning our program of work I hope we will not do it in this chamber. We should go to the farmers and have the farmers come to us. In this way I think we will be able to work out a program to make the agricultural industry viable again. Perhaps we can elevate this industry to an advanced position through technology. In this way perhaps we can increase the income of those who participate in agriculture.' .	3	ii b

I have no fault to find with the member for Laval.
In any case, I clearly have the impression that Quebec farmers will keep on worrying
Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies about them representation and questioning the commitments made during an election campaign, namely that they would be given the consideration they deserve in Canada.
I would like, for a few minutes, to go back 20 years when I was working in a slaughter house, which gave me the opportunity to meet many farmers and to talk with them. Things were not easy in those days. The difficulties were many, and we would always hope that our leaders and our governments would find solutions capable of improving the lot of farmers.
This was a time-many will remember it better than I-when many farmers, on the occasion of the Christmas and New Year's festivities-some might think it is funny, but it was nevertheless more serious for others- would slaughter one of their cows to feed their families.
And if we consider what has happened in the last 20 years, we notice that most of the farmers have not improved their lot, very much, since on account of the present policy, the farmer has to sell for instance not only one cow occasionally but must get rid of the whole herd.
This debate gives us the opportunity to express certain opinions and to ask the minister to consider more thoroughly possible solutions to the problems of the agricultural community. Some will say it is not an easy task, but one must not infer therefrom that it is an impossible one. I am not so unkind as to say that the minister is the only one responsible for the present state of affairs, but he will surely need the advice of his experts and will have to resort to the solutions that all hon. members are prepared to bring forward.
I say with pleasure to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) that we have heard for a long time about a new dairy policy providing price support for certain products, but nothing tangible is ever done.
In the province of Quebec the situation is uncertain, but it must not be better in New Brunswick where people have to sell potatoes at 60 cents for 75 pounds. I wonder how the potato producers will be able to pull themselves out of that again this year. Try as they may to make the potato producers and other farmers believe that they will eventually adopt a price policy, I believe they will have to act as soon as possible if they want their position to improve.
May I bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) the situation of the
November 18, 1969

Alleged Lack of Agricultural Policies tobacco growers. We have talked about several areas of production but the growers of cigarette tobacco, whether in, Ontario or in Quebec, are facing serious difficulties which slow down the development of this very important industry and I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to discuss the matter thoroughly with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) and to make him soften his stand.
Incidentally, I would like to commend the Minister of Agriculture who last year granted additional subsidies to improve the soils and to increase the acreage devoted to growing tobacco in some areas of the country. On the other hand, I am very much concerned, and so are the tobacco growers, about the stand taken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It is the second time I stress the point for I believe this industry is of major importance for some areas in Canada.
In my constituency there are more than 95 per cent of the cigarette tobacco growers of the whole province of Quebec, this means that it is an area more important still than Ontario in this respect, in spite of the great number of major tobacco producers in the latter province. While it is one of the very few productions able to survive without any government assistance, the attitude displayed by the minister during this past year is bound to be of great concern to us since the future of this industry is at stake.
I hope that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) will answer a request I made not so long ago when I asked him how much money he was getting from that industry.
[DOT] (9:4C p.m.)
Of course we are willing to help the Minister of National Health and Welfare fight against abuses which, unfortunately, are not restricted to the use of cigarettes.
All hon. members agree that abuses must be checked, but there is no conclusive proof that cigarettes cause cancer. Several other products would probably have the same effect. I dare hope that the Minister of Agriculture will see to it that tobacco growers no longer have cause for worry, that they can count not only on the government but on all hon. members to continue operating in an industry that enables many Canadian citizens to earn a living.
I would also like to say a few words on the responsibilities of the Canadian Dairy Commission. For a long time, the milk producers

have asked for an emergency debate, but the government did not think it was advisable to hold it. Personally, I agree entirely with the dairy producers who asked that their government explain clearly the policy of the Commission.
It is unfortunate to note that the Canadian Dairy Commission has been entrusted with the announcement of some kind of policy that is every year a bit more harsh and drastic. It is even suggested that there are 2,000 or 2,500 milk producers too many, but the officials have not yet had the courage to say it quite clearly, for reasons of political expediency.
However, the Canadian Dairy Commission is acting as the mouthpiece of the government, and I wonder if we cannot demand that our leaders have at least the courage and the honesty to explain clearly the dairy policy and to make the producers-however small- understand that they can no longer maintain their activity.

What do I think of it? I think that the existence of a surplus was too easily admitted and that nobody thought of using it by providing all the school boys of our country with free milk.
Furthermore, why should we not attempt to process this milk to feed cattle, as was done successfully in the United States? In Canada, we talked about it a year ago but nothing was done. I wonder if the government intends to do something in that respect. If it were simply a matter for an individual member of a rural riding to make such a recommendation, I would feel privileged to suggest it. As the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce must be very interested in the development of the tobacco industry, I wonder what will become of that support price policy and the restrictions on imports. To talk about it is not enough, action should follow.
I am deeply convinced that one of the ways to help the producers would be to limit our imports of truck-farm products. The committee on agriculture on which sit a number of government members, recognized that fact. It was noted, for instance, that on the south side we had 50,000 acres of humus-a black dirt very good for truck gardening-of which
15,000	acres only are in cultivation. It goes without saying that a policy restricting imports of such products would enable Quebecers to till the soil to its full capacity and thus lead a more decent life.
